A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same calibration study. All 11 pages of v1 and 18 pages of v2, including their appendices, are readable. Retained experiments, prompts, tables, and figures can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original SimpleQA experiments with six LLMs, including accuracy, calibration, distractor effects, question-type analyses, and human validation of the automated judge.

after.justification: v2 retains those results and reports additional experiments across nine LLMs and three datasets, plus a manual distractor-quality assessment.

M1.justification: The free-generation and distractor procedures remain unchanged: GPT-4o-mini generates three distractors, the correct answer and distractors are shuffled, and models provide answers and confidence scores. Appendix A's three prompts match after whitespace normalization. Added equations and model evaluations do not introduce a new method component.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from SimpleQA alone to SimpleQA, FaVIQ information-seeking questions, and TriviaQA open-domain trivia. FaVIQ uses support-labeled examples as factual QA; TriviaQA is evaluated without retrieved supporting context. These add substantially different question distributions within factual QA.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains the original six models and adds LLaMA-3-70B-8192, LLaMA-4-Scout-17B, and Qwen-QwQ-32B in both prompting settings. The appendix comparison using each answering model as its own judge retains the original six-model membership.

E3.justification: New evaluations specify 2,922 support-labeled FaVIQ R-test examples and the first 1,000 TriviaQA no-content validation questions. v2 also introduces a 500-plus-example distractor audit and explicit accuracy/ECE-change summaries. The original SimpleQA setup, prompting, judging rules, and 0.1-wide ECE bins remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Sections 4.3–4.4 add observational comparisons of tuning regimes, architectures, and scale within model families. The question-type analysis extends to the added models, and Appendix C reports a manual plausibility audit of over 500 SimpleQA examples. The earlier judge comparison and human validation are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report the same validation involving 100 responses, three human annotators, and Cohen's kappa of 0.82 in Appendix B. Neither reports repeated-run variability, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new distractor audit does not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: The original six-model SimpleQA results and appendix judge-comparison values are retained. v2 adds results for three models, two datasets, and expanded question-type comparisons. Newly reported TriviaQA results show GPT-4o accuracy increasing from 89.66% to 95.55% under distractors while ECE worsens from 0.071 to 0.083; these are new-condition results, not improvements over v1.

T1.justification: Section 3.1's equations formalize the prompting procedure already described in v1. The helped/harmed conditions and standard accuracy/ECE-difference formulas make existing comparisons explicit. No substantive new mathematical assumptions, theoretical results, proofs, or derivations are introduced.

C1.justification: The contribution scope expands to a unified nine-model, three-dataset benchmark and a claim of independently disentangling scale, tuning, and architecture. The abstract and conclusion newly emphasize that distractors can worsen calibration on easier questions, qualifying the earlier general account of their benefits.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving confidence inflation on easy questions, training-data differences, RLHF, distillation, and architecture. It develops different deployment recommendations by model size and explicitly identifies synthetic-distractor realism and untested multi-hop/generative tasks as limitations. These substantially extend v1's size and question-type interpretations.

D1.justification: Section 3.3 and Appendix D/Table 3 replace brief model descriptions with detailed documentation of parameter counts, context windows, architectures, pretraining data volumes, and tuning regimes. v2 also supplies dataset filtering, sampling, and question-type counts. The original prompts and code/data access link are retained; the added model documentation does not establish changed training.

R1.justification: A dedicated Related Work section substantially expands positioning around intrinsic calibration, training, alignment, and post-hoc methods. New cognitive-psychology references motivate distractors through considering alternative answers. Several earlier citations, including Kapoor et al. and Ulmer et al., are removed, while the claimed research gap becomes more explicitly centered on structured distractor settings.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Experimental setup and results are reorganized into numbered thematic subsections, and related work receives its own section. The appendices are reorganized and expanded while preserving the original prompts and judge analysis.

P2.justification: Table 1 becomes a multi-dataset comparison, and the main reliability figure expands from six to nine panels while dropping bar-count annotations. v2 adds accuracy/ECE-change plots and appendix reliability diagrams, and merges the expanded question-type table and redrawn radar plots into Figure 4. The original judge-comparison displays are retained with relocation and renumbering.

improvement.justification: Moving beyond v1's single benchmark provides useful evidence that accuracy gains can coexist with worse calibration on TriviaQA. The distractor audit and clearer organization also help. These gains are tempered by claims of independently isolating model factors through heterogeneous-model comparisons and inconsistent reporting: the abstract's maximum accuracy gain of 460% conflicts with approximately 819% in Figure 3.
